examples.title: One iteration of k-means by hand
examples.prompt: Ten ages are 20, 21, 22, 28, 35, 40, 41, 42, 43 and 44. Run one iteration of k-means with \(k=2\) and starting centroids \(c_1=21\) and \(c_2=30\). Give each age its cluster label and find the new centroids.

steps.say: Start from the two given centroids, 21 and 30 years.
With one feature the Euclidean distance is just the size of the difference, so each age gets two distances.
Ages 20, 21 and 22 are closer to 21, so they join cluster 1. Age 28 is 2 away from 30 but 7 away from 21, so it joins cluster 2 with every older age.
Each centroid moves to the mean of its members. Cluster 1 keeps its centroid at 21, while cluster 2 moves from 30 up to 39.
After one iteration the clusters are 20 to 22 and 28 to 44, with centroids 21 and 39. A second iteration would move 28 into cluster 1, because 28 is now closer to 21.

examples.title: Classify a new object with K-NN
examples.prompt: Surgical mesh from four vendors was graded Pass or Fail by surgeons. A new vendor has strength \(x_1=7\) kg/m² and flexibility \(x_2=3\). Classify it with K-NN using \(K=3\) and the Euclidean distance, and give the probability that it fails.

steps.say: Strength runs from 4 to 7 and flexibility from 1 to 7, so both features are on similar small scales and are used as they are.
Subtract the matching features, square, add and take the square root for each vendor.
C is nearest, then D and then A. B is the farthest, so it is left out when K is 3.
Two of the three neighbors failed, so the new mesh is classified as Fail.
Two of the three votes are Fail, so the probability that the new mesh fails is 2 in 3.
